lessons.title: Introduction to Home Economics
objectives: Explain in simple words what Home Economics is.
Identify everyday activities related to Home Economics.
State one way the subject can help pupils at home and at school.
lessons.lesson: Home Economics teaches useful knowledge and practical skills for caring for ourselves, our families and our homes. It includes learning about food, clothing, personal cleanliness and keeping the home environment safe and tidy. Pupils already meet Home Economics ideas in everyday life when they wash their hands, keep their uniforms clean, help arrange a room or choose healthy foods. The subject helps us make sensible choices and use time and materials carefully.
examples: Washing hands before eating.
Folding clean clothes.
Keeping food covered and the kitchen tidy.
lessons.activity: Pupils name safe, age-appropriate tasks they can do at home or school and group them under food, clothing, personal care and home care.
evaluation: What is Home Economics?
Name three activities related to Home Economics.
Give one way Home Economics can help you at home.

lessons.title: Scope, Importance and Careers in Home Economics
objectives: Explain the meaning of Home Economics.
Name areas studied in Home Economics.
State ways Home Economics helps individuals and families.
Identify careers connected with Home Economics.
lessons.lesson: Home Economics covers food and nutrition, clothing and textiles, personal care, home care and family living. It teaches people to make sensible choices, keep their surroundings clean, use resources wisely and develop useful practical skills. It can help families plan meals, care for clothes, maintain a safe home and manage everyday resources. Careers related to the subject include catering, cooking, fashion design, tailoring, nutrition work and home-care services.
examples: Planning a simple healthy meal is part of food and nutrition.
Mending a loose button is part of clothing care.
A caterer prepares food for people.
lessons.activity: In small groups, pupils sort picture cards into food, clothing, personal care and home-care activities. Each group names one way the activity helps a family.
evaluation: What is Home Economics?
Name four areas of Home Economics.
State three ways Home Economics is useful.
Mention two careers related to the subject.

lessons.title: The Human Body: Parts and Their Functions
objectives: Identify major external parts of the human body.
State simple functions of selected body parts.
Explain why the body should be cared for.
lessons.lesson: The human body has many parts that work together. The head contains the brain, eyes, ears, nose and mouth. The eyes help us see, the ears help us hear, the nose helps us smell and the mouth helps us eat and speak. The trunk contains important organs, while the arms and hands help us lift, hold and carry things. The legs and feet help us stand, walk and run. We care for our bodies through bathing, clean clothing, healthy food, exercise and rest.
examples: Hands help us hold a pencil.
Legs help us walk to school.
The mouth helps us chew food and speak.
lessons.activity: Pupils label a simple body outline and match body parts with their functions. No pupil should be asked to disclose private body information.
evaluation: Name five external parts of the body.
What do the eyes, ears and nose help us do?
Give three ways of caring for the body.

lessons.title: Food and Nutrition
objectives: Explain the meaning of food and nutrition.
Give reasons people eat food.
Identify examples of foods commonly eaten in the locality.
lessons.lesson: Food is what we eat or drink to supply the body with nutrients and energy. Nutrition is the process by which the body takes in and uses food. We eat to obtain energy, grow, repair body tissues and protect ourselves from illness. Common foods in Nigerian communities include rice, yam, beans, maize, vegetables, fruits, fish, eggs and milk. A healthy diet contains different kinds of food in suitable amounts, together with clean drinking water.
examples: Beans and eggs help the body grow and repair itself.
Rice and yam provide energy.
Oranges and leafy vegetables supply protective nutrients.
lessons.activity: Pupils list foods eaten at home and sort them into broad food groups. Discuss how local foods can form a balanced meal.
evaluation: What is food?
Explain nutrition in your own words.
Give four reasons people eat food.
Name five foods commonly eaten in your locality.

lessons.title: The Six Classes of Food and Their Sources
objectives: Name the six classes of food.
Give examples and sources of each class.
State a simple function of each class.
lessons.lesson: The six classes of food are carbohydrates, proteins, fats and oils, vitamins, minerals and water. Carbohydrates provide energy and are found in foods such as rice, yam and maize. Proteins support growth and repair; examples include beans, fish, eggs and meat. Fats and oils provide stored energy and are found in vegetable oil, groundnuts and some seeds. Vitamins and minerals help the body work properly and are found in fruits, vegetables, milk and other foods. Water helps digestion and keeps the body hydrated.
examples: Carbohydrate: yam.
Protein: beans.
Fat and oil: groundnut oil.
Vitamins: oranges and carrots.
Minerals: milk and leafy vegetables.
Water: safe drinking water.
lessons.activity: Groups arrange food picture cards under the six classes. Emphasise that a food may contain more than one nutrient.
evaluation: List the six classes of food.
Give two sources of protein.
What is one function of carbohydrates?
Why should we drink clean water?

lessons.title: Kitchen Equipment and Utensils: Uses and Care
objectives: Explain the difference between kitchen equipment and utensils.
Identify common kitchen items and their uses.
Describe safe ways to clean and store kitchen items.
lessons.lesson: Kitchen equipment and utensils are items used to prepare, cook, serve and store food. Equipment may include a cooker, refrigerator, blender or weighing scale. Utensils include spoons, ladles, knives, plates, cups and cooking pots. After use, items should be washed with clean water and suitable soap, rinsed and dried. Sharp tools should be handled carefully and stored safely. Electrical equipment must be switched off and unplugged by an adult before cleaning.
examples: A pot is used for cooking food.
A ladle is used for serving soup.
A refrigerator helps keep food cold.
lessons.activity: Pupils identify safe, clean kitchen items shown by the teacher and match each item to its use. Demonstrate washing and safe storage using unbreakable classroom props.
evaluation: What are kitchen utensils?
Name three pieces of kitchen equipment.
State two differences between equipment and utensils.
Mention four ways to care for kitchen items.

lessons.title: Needle Craft: Meaning, Articles and Basic Practice
objectives: Explain the meaning of needle craft.
Identify simple articles made with needle and thread.
Demonstrate safe, simple threading and stitching under teacher supervision.
lessons.lesson: Needle craft means making or repairing useful items with a needle, thread or related materials. It can be used to join pieces of cloth, decorate fabric or repair a small tear. Articles made through needle craft include handkerchiefs, simple cloth bags, table mats and decorative pieces. A needle is sharp, so pupils must work while seated, follow the teacher's instructions and return needles to a safe container after use.
examples: Sewing a loose button back onto a shirt.
Joining two pieces of fabric to make a small pouch.
lessons.activity: The teacher demonstrates threading a large blunt-ended practice needle and making a simple running stitch on a fabric card. Pupils practise only with age-appropriate tools under direct supervision.
evaluation: What is needle craft?
Name three articles made with needle craft.
Why must needles be handled carefully?

lessons.title: Simple Sewing Tools and Their Uses
objectives: Identify common simple sewing tools.
State the use of each tool.
Describe how to keep sewing tools safely.
lessons.lesson: Simple sewing tools help people measure, cut, join and mark fabric. A tape measure measures cloth and body measurements. Scissors cut fabric or thread. Needles carry thread through cloth. Thread joins pieces of fabric. A thimble protects a finger while sewing, and pins hold cloth pieces together temporarily. Tools should be counted before and after practical work, kept dry and stored in a closed sewing box away from small children.
examples: Tape measure: measuring cloth.
Scissors: cutting fabric.
Needle and thread: joining cloth.
lessons.activity: Pupils match labelled tool pictures to their functions. The teacher demonstrates safe passing and storage of scissors and needles.
evaluation: Name five sewing tools.
What is a tape measure used for?
How should needles and scissors be stored?

lessons.title: Knitting and Crocheting: Meaning, Tools and Articles
objectives: Explain knitting and crocheting in simple terms.
Identify basic tools used for each craft.
Name articles that can be made by knitting or crocheting.
lessons.lesson: Knitting and crocheting are crafts used to make fabric and useful articles by joining loops of yarn. Knitting commonly uses two needles, while crocheting commonly uses one hooked needle called a crochet hook. Yarn or wool is the material used. People make items such as caps, scarves, sweaters, small bags and decorative pieces. Beginners should start with simple patterns and work patiently under guidance.
examples: A knitted scarf.
A crocheted small mat.
A woollen cap.
lessons.activity: Pupils examine safe samples of knitted and crocheted items and identify visible loops. The teacher demonstrates the tools without requiring pupils to use sharp or unsuitable equipment.
evaluation: What is knitting?
What is crocheting?
Name one tool used in crocheting.
List three articles made by knitting or crocheting.

lessons.title: Revision: Food Classes, Nutrients and Nutrition
objectives: Recall the six classes of food.
Explain why the body needs different nutrients.
Group familiar foods by their main nutrient.
lessons.lesson: People need different nutrients because the body has different jobs to perform. Carbohydrates and fats provide energy; proteins help growth and repair; vitamins and minerals support healthy body functions; and water helps the body work properly. A balanced diet contains a variety of foods in suitable amounts. No single food supplies everything the body needs, so meals should include different food groups.
examples: Rice with beans and vegetables provides a wider range of nutrients than rice alone.
Clean water should be taken regularly.
lessons.activity: Pupils plan a simple local meal using foods from at least three food groups.
evaluation: Name the six classes of food.
Why is a balanced diet important?
Suggest a balanced meal using foods found locally.

lessons.title: Methods of Cooking: Boiling
objectives: Explain boiling as a method of cooking.
Identify foods that can be boiled.
State basic safety rules for boiling food.
lessons.lesson: Boiling is a method of cooking food in water or another suitable liquid heated until it bubbles. It is used for foods such as yam, rice, eggs, beans and some vegetables. Food should be cleaned and prepared before cooking. A pot should not be filled too high, and the handle should be turned away from the edge of the cooker. Only an adult should handle hot pots, boiling water and cooking flames.
examples: Boiled yam.
Boiled eggs.
Rice cooked in water.
lessons.activity: The teacher demonstrates the stages of boiling using a safe cooking demonstration or pictures. Pupils sequence the steps without handling hot equipment.
evaluation: What is boiling?
Name four foods that can be boiled.
State three safety rules for boiling food.

lessons.title: Methods of Cooking: Roasting
objectives: Explain roasting as a method of cooking.
Identify foods that can be roasted.
Describe safety precautions when roasting.
lessons.lesson: Roasting is cooking food with dry heat, usually over or near a source of heat or inside an oven. Foods that may be roasted include plantain, corn, yam, fish and meat. Food should be prepared hygienically and cooked properly. Roasting must be done by an adult or under close adult supervision because fire, hot surfaces and smoke can cause burns or breathing problems.
examples: Roasted plantain.
Roasted corn.
Fish roasted by an adult.
lessons.activity: Pupils compare pictures of boiled and roasted foods and describe differences in appearance and preparation. The teacher discusses fire safety.
evaluation: What is roasting?
Name three foods that can be roasted.
Why should pupils not handle open fire or hot roasting equipment?

lessons.title: Personal Grooming and Safe Personal Care
objectives: Explain personal grooming.
Identify safe ways to care for the body.
Recognise that cosmetics and chemicals must be used safely.
lessons.lesson: Personal grooming means keeping the body clean, neat and presentable. Good grooming includes bathing, brushing the teeth, washing the hands, keeping nails clean, combing the hair and wearing clean clothes. Some adults use personal-care products such as creams or deodorants, but products must be suitable for the person and used according to their labels. Pupils should not share personal products or apply unknown chemicals to their skin.
examples: Washing hands with soap after using the toilet.
Brushing teeth with a suitable toothbrush and toothpaste.
Wearing clean clothes.
lessons.activity: Pupils arrange picture cards into a daily personal-care routine. Discuss why unknown creams, bleaching products and strong chemicals should not be used.
evaluation: What is personal grooming?
List five good grooming habits.
Why should pupils avoid unknown cosmetics and chemicals?

lessons.title: Personal Clothing: Types and Care
objectives: Identify common types of personal clothing.
Explain why clothing should be cared for.
Describe simple steps for washing, drying, ironing and storing clothes.
lessons.lesson: Personal clothing includes shirts, dresses, trousers, skirts, uniforms, underwear, socks and footwear. Clothes protect the body, provide comfort and help people dress appropriately for different activities. Caring for clothes helps them remain clean and last longer. Care includes sorting dirty clothes, washing them with suitable soap, rinsing, drying properly, ironing with adult supervision, mending small tears and storing clothes neatly. Care labels should be followed where available.
examples: A school uniform should be washed and dried before it is worn again.
Shoes should be cleaned and stored in a dry place.
lessons.activity: Pupils sequence picture cards showing the safe steps for caring for clothes. The teacher demonstrates folding a clean garment.
evaluation: Name five types of personal clothing.
Give three reasons for caring for clothes.
List the steps for washing and storing clothes.

lessons.title: Reasons for Wearing Clothes
objectives: State reasons people wear clothes.
Match clothing to weather and activities.
Explain why clean and suitable clothing is important.
lessons.lesson: People wear clothes to protect the body from heat, cold, rain, dust and injury. Clothes also provide comfort, help people meet cultural or school expectations and may identify a role or occupation. Different weather and activities require suitable clothing. Light, breathable clothes may be more comfortable in hot weather, while warmer clothes help in cold conditions. Protective clothing is used for certain jobs and activities.
examples: A raincoat helps keep the body dry in rain.
A school uniform identifies pupils at school.
A safety helmet protects the head when required.
lessons.activity: Pupils match clothing pictures to weather conditions and activities, explaining their choices.
evaluation: Give four reasons people wear clothes.
What clothing may be suitable on a rainy day?
Why should clothing be clean and appropriate?

lessons.title: Liquid Soap: Uses and Safe Preparation Concepts
objectives: State common uses of liquid soap.
Identify safe, ordinary materials used for handwashing.
Explain why hazardous soap-making chemicals must only be handled by trained adults.
lessons.lesson: Liquid soap is a cleaning product used for washing hands and some surfaces. Soap helps loosen dirt and oils so they can be rinsed away with water. For a Primary 4 classroom activity, use a commercially prepared liquid soap or a teacher-prepared, low-risk mixture made from ordinary soap flakes and water. Some industrial soap-making ingredients, including caustic soda and strong acids, can cause severe burns and must never be handled by pupils. Do not mix unknown cleaning chemicals.
examples: Washing hands with liquid soap and clean running water.
Using a labelled household soap according to its instructions.
lessons.activity: Pupils demonstrate the correct handwashing sequence using ready-made liquid soap. The teacher explains hazard symbols and why strong chemicals are restricted to trained adults.
evaluation: Give two uses of liquid soap.
How does soap help remove dirt?
Why must pupils not handle caustic soda or strong acids?

lessons.title: Uses and Care of Simple Sewing Tools
objectives: Recall common sewing tools.
Explain how each tool is used.
Demonstrate safe storage and care of sewing tools.
lessons.lesson: Sewing tools are useful only when they are clean, safe and in good condition. Scissors should be kept dry and closed when not in use. Needles and pins should be counted and stored in a pincushion or closed container. Tape measures should be rolled neatly rather than pulled or knotted. Thread should be kept dry and free from dust. Pupils should use tools only with the teacher's permission and supervision.
examples: Store needles in a closed needle case.
Wipe and close scissors after use.
Keep thread in a dry sewing box.
lessons.activity: Pupils inspect pictures of well-kept and poorly kept sewing tools, identify hazards and suggest improvements.
evaluation: State three ways to care for sewing tools.
Why should needles be counted after a practical lesson?
How should scissors be stored?

lessons.title: Stitches and Their Types
objectives: Explain what a stitch is.
Distinguish temporary, permanent and decorative stitches.
Identify simple examples of each type.
lessons.lesson: A stitch is a loop or pass of thread made with a needle through fabric. Temporary stitches hold pieces of cloth in position for a short time and can be removed later. Permanent stitches are used to join fabric more firmly. Decorative stitches are used to make patterns or improve the appearance of cloth. Examples include running stitch, backstitch and simple decorative patterns. Practical work should use age-appropriate needles and close teacher supervision.
examples: A temporary running stitch used to hold a seam before final sewing.
A permanent backstitch used to join fabric.
A decorative stitch used to form a pattern.
lessons.activity: Pupils compare teacher-prepared stitch samples and classify them as temporary, permanent or decorative.
evaluation: What is a stitch?
Name the three broad types of stitches.
Give one use of a temporary stitch and one use of a permanent stitch.
